projectOutComesReport:
This project has achieved significant breakthroughs towards solving one of the canonical challenges in computer vision and graphics, namely inverse rendering, in the very challenging setting of indoor scenes. Inverse rendering requires simultaneous estimation of shape, material and lighting, which is difficult in indoor scenes where shapes can be arbitrary, material properties are complex and light sources influence the appearance of distant parts of the scene. We develop physically-based deep networks to estimate shape, material and especially lighting with unprecedented detail, by accounting for visibilities in a single image, consistency in multiple images and complex light transport in challenging or dynamic scenes. This has enabled novel applications in augmented reality and image editing, such as view synthesis, object insertion, as well as material and light source editing, using just a single or few images.

Our results have been published at leading venues in computer vision and graphics, including CVPR, ECCV, ICCV, SIGGRAPH and SIGGRAPH Asia. A few highlight results in these papers include: (a) the first method for editing light sources in indoor scenes to allow full scene relighting, (b) a factorization approach to relight indoor scenes with high specularity that is significantly faster than previous methods, (c) diffusion models for texture synthesis, (d) methods and datasets for multi-illumination inverse rendering, (e) spatiotemporal consistency in indoor inverse rendering that enables photorealistic object insertion and relighting with a single video as input.

The grant has shaped the PhD thesis research of multiple students advised by the PI and co-PI, several of whom won prestigious awards such as the Google PhD Fellowship and the Qualcomm Innovation Fellowship. Students also won the ECCV 2022 Best Paper Honorable Mention and the Best Paper Award at EGSR 2024. Undergraduate research teams from backgrounds that are traditionally disadvantaged in computer science have been mentored by the PIs as part of the Early Research Scholars Program. The grant has enabled the development of coursework at UCSD, including CSE 152A, CSE 152B, CSE 167 and CSE 168 on undergraduate computer vision and graphics, as well as CSE 252D which teaches the state-of-the-art in computer vision, including topics like inverse rendering, neural rendering, vision-language models and diffusion models.

abstractText:
This Major Research Instrumentation Award is for a 3D Small-Angle and Wide-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS/WAXS) instrument, located in a shared nano/microfabrication and materials analysis facility at UC San Diego. As an essential analytical tool, this advanced SAXS/WAXS instrument supports the ongoing research of a broad cross-section of researchers, enabling discoveries in synthetic chemistry, catalysis, inorganic and biological materials, quantum materials, and energy storage/conversion materials. The instrument provides a versatile, state-of-the-art, reliable and local solution to the SAXS needs of the large scientific community in the Southern California region comprising San Diego and Orange Counties. In addition, the SAXS/WAXS instrument is used to enrich the training of both graduate and undergraduate students in the theory, synthesis, and analysis of nano- and microstructured materials. It allows instructors to use modern research data for pedagogical purposes, provides students with hands-on x-ray training to enhance their science, engineering, and technology curriculum, and augments the educational outreach programs at UC San Diego, bringing a significant opportunity to increase participation of underrepresented students in research.

Small-Angle and Wide-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS/WAXS) is one of the few experimental techniques that can characterize the nano- and microstructure of soft matter and nanomaterials. It is an essential analytical tool in the characterization of mesoscale and nanoscale features in a wide range of biological and artificial materials. The instrument enables measurement in a dynamic environment (with in-situ control of temperature, humidity, and ambient gas concentration) to provide insights into materials structure-function and structure-response relationships. Unique features of the instrument include automated simultaneous SAXS and WAXS measurements, grazing incidence measurements on liquid interfaces, and low-volume flow-through sampling of biomacromolecules. These features are also appropriate for studies of: (i) short-lived species; (ii) degradation-prone biological samples; (iii) air-, temperature-, or water-sensitive materials; and (iv) materials systems that require frequent or long-timescale x-ray measurements. The instrument also features a doubly focused point source, which allows for collecting scattering data from both isotropic and anisotropic samples because a scattering image can be generated from the entire projected source. The instrument is used to solve transformational materials science problems in the areas of mesomaterials, inorganic, and biological materials, quantum materials, and energy storage/conversion materials.

projectOutComesReport:
This project provided a versatile, state-of-the-art, reliable and local solution to the Small Angle and Wide-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS/WAXS) needs of the scientific community at UC San Diego and in the greater Southern California area. SAXS/WAXS is one of the few experimental techniques that can characterize the nano- and microstructure of soft-matter and nanomaterials, and it is an essential analytical tool in the characterization of mesoscale and nanoscale features in a wide range of biological and artificial materials. This project acquired and established a 3D Small Angle and Wide-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS/WAXS) instrument as a valuable and accessible resource that for research and education.

Intellectual Merit:

This award supported the acquisition of a Xeuss 3.0 with Genix 3D system made by Xenocs Inc. that is capable of sampling a diverse range of materials and molecular systems, equipped with SAXS/WAXS and grazing incidence SAXS/WAXS capabilities, and provides flexibility for integration with other inline measurements (e.g. UV-vis, HPLC). The instrument was received and installed at UC San Diego in late February 2023. It is currently housed in the Center for Memory Research and Recording at UC San Diego, which has established a modern X-ray user facility for materials characterization. The acquired Xeuss 3.0 has provided the solution of several transformational materials science problems and exciting discoveries in synthetic chemistry, catalysis, inorganic and biological materials, quantum materials, and energy storage/conversion materials. This includes: the dissolution dynamics and structure of crystalline polymer-ferritin hybrid materials; in-depth electrolyte performance analysis in Li-based batteries; the anisotropic structure of nanocrystal assemblies; the mesoscale structure of hyperbolic materials made by self-assembly; the internal structure of swollen hydrogels.

Broader Impacts:

Acquisition of an advanced SAXS/WAXS instrument has dramatically elevated the ongoing research programs of a broad cross-section of researchers in the southern California region. Since installation in 2023,  this instrument has provided training for 14 unique users and has logged over 750 user hours. Multiple workshops utilizing the SAXS/WAXS instrument provided training opportunities for 3 full-time engineers/research associates, 2 postdocs, and 10 graduate students over the lifetime of this award. The instrument has enriched the training of both graduate and undergraduate students in the theory, synthesis and analysis of nano- and microstructured materials and provided unique hands-on training in X-ray characterization for summer undergraduate researchers on the UC San Diego campus.

abstractText:
Energy storage devices that offer fast charging and long lifetime are essential for powering wireless electronics in our daily lives. This award supports fundamental research on energy storage technologies based on structural supercapacitors, which will potentially provide high peak power for rapid charging and extend device lifetime to minimize maintenance costs. Structural supercapacitors are multi-functional devices that integrates mechanical and electrochemical functions, reducing weight and maximizing the use of structural space to increase the available energy capacity. However, there are knowledge gaps on how to design and fabricate this class of devices. This project will contribute new knowledge related to electrodeposition processing that enables precise tuning of materials and device structures to attain unprecedented energy density and mechanical strength in a new generation of structural supercapacitors.  The research and outreach activities will engage under-represented students and foster the training and development of a future diverse workforce that works towards energy sustainability, promoting our national welfare and prosperity.

The goal of this research is to precisely create hierarchical composites and attain the desired mechanical and electrochemical attributes by building on uniquely stable redox polymers and scalable electrodeposition techniques. The research team will establish systematic design principles for the cell subcomponents (electrodes and electrolytes) and, when the cell is put together, examine the entire structure by ultrasound diagnostics to understand interfacial interactions and evaluate the cell multifunctional efficiency. Non-destructive, low-cost ultrasound techniques will directly probe the device mechanical properties and reveal their changes over time, particularly to identify chemical versus structural degradation mechanisms that must be mitigated to achieve long cycle life and highly durable systems. This project merges the fields of electrochemical storage with material mechanics in convergence research, to deliver structure-processing-property relationships for organic structural supercapacitors and a blueprint for practical fabrication processes compatible with manufacturing in the future. The project will also allow the principal investigator to enhance her research program through partnerships with investigators at other institutions, building expertise to address the challenges of fabricating structural energy storage devices.

projectOutComesReport:
This project advanced research on materials and processing for structural supercapacitors, which are multi-functional devices that combine load-bearing and energy-storage functions. By optimizing structural space, these devices increased energy capacity and achieved weight savings. The project developed novel strategies to improve properties of the electrodes and electrolyte. The structural electrodes were reinforced by coating carbon fibers with redox-stable polymers that raised electrochemical capacitance and mechanical strength. The solid polymer electrolytes were engineered with a gradient structure enabling fast ion transport while maintaining device durability. The devices were successfully demonstrated in various applications, delivering high peak power for rapid charging and an extended device lifetime to reduce maintenance costs. The project outcomes included six peer-reviewed publications, one patent applicaiton, and presentations at scientific conferences hosted by the American Chemical Society, Materials Research Society, and Electrochemical Society.

Regarding the broader impacts of this project, PI Ng mentored three PhD students, one MS student, and three undergraduate summer interns on this project, contributing to workforce development. With the support of this award, the PI and two students participated in the NSF I-Corps entrepreneurial training program to translate research outcomes towards technology commercialization. The project has facilitated the PI to establish partnerships and sabbatical visits with investigators at other institutions, strengthening the research network to address the challenges in energy storage technologies.

abstractText:
Group testing is a screening technique that relies on careful combinatorial mixing and testing of batches of samples. By using group testing instead of individual testing, for most problem settings of practical interest, one is guaranteed significant savings in the number of tests performed and consequently, significant reductions in reporting delays and experimental costs. Group testing is especially desirable when monitoring the spread of infectious diseases such as Covid-19, which requires frequent examinations of massive populations. Although many ad-hoc approaches to group testing for infectious diseases have been put forward, little work has addressed the problem of end-to-end group-testing protocol design, which includes the selection of genetic regions for viral/bacterial identification, mathematical modeling and analysis of the test results and the development of guiding protocols for communal testing strategies. The overarching goals of the project are to determine which group-testing methods can actually mitigate the spread of Covid-19 and other diseases and to what extent, to estimate the reduction in the number of infected individuals achievable through the use of pooled real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) tests, and to aid in the employment of Mobile Testing Units that can reach geographically remote regions. Other broader societal impacts include increased readiness for fighting future pandemics and training a new cohort of young researchers on interdisciplinary topics involving machine learning, coding theory and bioinformatics. 

The project aims to develop specialized machine-learning, combinatorial and information-theoretic methods for (a) identifying genomic regions with predictably low-mutation rates that may be used as amplification primers for gold-standard real-time polymerase chain reactions (RT-PCR) and determining best mixing strategies based on the likelihood of infection; (b) developing adequate models for amplification curves generated by RT-PCR and corresponding test-errors; (c) formulating experimental-protocol-specific non-adaptive and adaptive semiquantitative group testing schemes that account for nonbinary test outcomes; (d) addressing the testing issues associated with high-viral load subjects and heavy-hitter communities; and (e) integrating the mathematical techniques developed into an agent-based model for disease spreading and control in order to assess the potential impact of group testing and recommend effective test-quarantine-retest strategies.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
This Project Outcomes Report for the General Public is displayed verbatim as submitted by the Principal Investigator (PI) for this award. Any opinions, findings, and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this Report are those of the PI and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Science Foundation; NSF has not approved or endorsed its content.

The rapid spread of infectious diseases, such as COVID-19, has highlighted the urgent need for efficient and scalable diagnostic testing strategies. Traditional approaches to testing, which often involve testing individuals one by one, are resource-intensive and can become impractical when large populations need frequent monitoring. Group testing offers a promising alternative by allowing multiple samples to be tested simultaneously in a combinatorial manner, significantly reducing the number of tests required while still accurately identifying infected individuals. Despite its potential, existing group testing techniques are primarily designed for binary outcomes (positive/negative) and do not fully utilize the semi-quantitative information available in many modern diagnostic techniques, such as real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR).

 This research effort aimed to advance the field of group testing by developing new methodologies that leverage semi-quantitative data to improve testing efficiency and accuracy. By incorporating richer information from test results, such as varying levels of viral load, we sought to design testing schemes that outperform traditional approaches, especially in settings with a small number of infected individuals or clustered outbreaks. Our work also explored novel connections between group testing, combinatorial mathematics, and information theory, including the use of tropical arithmetic and graph-theoretic techniques, to provide deeper insights into the tradeoffs between the number of tests performed, decoding complexity, and testing accuracy. Through these advancements, we aimed to enhance the ability to detect and control infectious disease outbreaks, while also contributing to the broader theoretical foundations of group testing and related disciplines.

 Our research yielded several significant theoretical advancements in the field of group testing, particularly in the development of nearly optimal semi-quantitative schemes and the exploration of new parameter regimes for both adaptive and non-adaptive settings. One of our key findings was the existence of nearly optimal semi-quantitative group testing schemes in settings where Ct (cycle threshold) values from RT-PCR tests were used to distinguish varying viral loads. Although a major challenge in this setting is that the Ct values of certain infected individuals can mask those of others, we were able to design schemes that not only accounted for this masking effect but also outperformed the information-theoretic lower bound for binary group testing when the number of infected individuals was small. This surprising result demonstrates the potential of semi-quantitative information to achieve efficiencies beyond traditional group testing methods. In the context of adaptive group testing, we further showed that it is possible to construct schemes that outperform the information-theoretic lower bound for binary group testing across any number of infected individuals. By leveraging the ability to sequentially update testing strategies based on previous results, we developed methods that significantly reduce the number of tests needed while maintaining high accuracy in identifying infected individuals. These results suggest that adaptive strategies can offer substantial improvements over non-adaptive counterparts, particularly when rich, semi-quantitative data are available.

 Additionally, we made important contributions to the theory of non-adaptive binary group testing, where the testing strategy is fixed in advance. We demonstrated that it is possible to identify a uniformly random subset of k infected individuals from a population of n using only \ln(2 - 4\epsilon)^{-2} k \ln n tests, with a decoding complexity of O(\epsilon^{-2} k \ln n) for any small \epsilon > 0. This result was achieved by utilizing Mobius transformations and generating functions, allowing for a more refined analysis of the tradeoffs between the number of tests and the decoding complexity. These findings expand the range of achievable parameters in non-adaptive group testing and provide new insights into the efficiency limits of combinatorial testing.

abstractText:
The connectivity solutions need to scale up massively to support unprecedented exponential growth in data rates and the number of devices. The primary approach to meet the demands has been to upgrade the infrastructure, such as adding base stations with multiple antennas and/or upgrading clients. Unfortunately, these approaches have fallen short of their goal as in practice, the channels between users and base stations have limited scattering or richness to enable spatial multiplexing, and users are not sufficiently separated in the spatial domain. This proposal will shape the channel to unlock the full potential of wireless networks without requiring updating the base station or user device at a low cost in terms of power and expense. The proposed research aims to adaptively modify and morph the wireless medium using smart passive reflector surfaces to materialize the spatial multiplexing gains. The underlying idea is to use smart reflectors to create additional channel diversity to manipulate the received signal before reflecting it to minimize interference at the receivers. The research brings together PIs and techniques from communications theory, networked system design, and antenna design to build scalable and low-cost wireless networks. The project also proposes a synergistic educational and outreach plan that leverages the technical work to build exciting demos for undergraduate and K-12 classrooms. For example, a smart surface-based demo, which increases the data rate and coverage of current Wi-Fi devices, will introduce students to the wonders of engineering in a pragmatic yet compelling way, with the hope of increasing diversity in STEM-related education environments.

The proposal would develop smart surface designs capable of morphing the channel, and develop the hardware prototype and algorithms to provide coverage and multiplexing gains to support massive numbers of users and the exponential increase in data rates. The designed smart surface with fine-grained control would allow us to morph the wireless channel or environment to increase the diversity and multiplexing gains as deemed necessary during optimization. We further establish smart surface placement theory and algorithms and quantify the performance-size trade-offs. We develop low-overhead channel estimation and low-latency optimization algorithms for the base station to support temporal channel changes and improve the data rate and connectivity. The proposed effort would develop the theory and algorithms for multi-user setups to ensure scalability with smart surfaces. The proposed work would enable the first low-cost, practical smart surface and algorithms supporting high-mobility users with significant data-rate improvements.

projectOutComesReport:
To address the growing demand for faster and more reliable wireless communications, this project explored a novel approach: reshaping the wireless environment itself using adaptive smart surfaces. Rather than upgrading base stations or user devices—which can be expensive and inefficient—we focused on modifying the wireless channel between them to enhance performance. Our research led to the development of a new class of “smart reflector surfaces” designed to improve network capacity in a cost-effective and scalable way.

At the heart of our findings are three classes of smart surfaces developed over the course of the project: two are purely passive, requiring no batteries or external power, and one incorporates active components. We explored the use of these surfaces to manipulate signal polarization, redirect wireless signals, and create constructive multipath reflections with phase shifts optimized to increase capacity. While passive smart surfaces can influence various aspects of the wireless channel, their practical impact is limited to short-range scenarios, with only modest improvements observed in real-world environments. As a result, we conclude that future Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) or Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS) should include active capabilities—such as signal amplification and dynamic control—to meaningfully enhance real-world wireless performance.

Intellectual Merit: Our study evaluated several smart surface prototypes for their ability to enhance the performance of MIMO (Multiple Input, Multiple Output) systems, which improve wireless capacity by transmitting multiple data streams simultaneously. We found that passive smart surfaces offered benefits primarily in controlled indoor settings, such as anechoic chambers. In more complex real-world environments, the channel typically includes one strong path along with multiple weak reflections—some of which help and others hinder communication. Passive surfaces helped mitigate these issues, but only when placed very close to access points or base stations. When placed farther away, their impact diminished significantly and they could not overcome channel limitations caused by polarization mismatch or low signal strength.

In the later stages of the project, we used simulations to analyze an active RIS design that featured circular polarization and per-element amplification. This active RIS demonstrated up to a 5 dB improvement in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and a 10 dB increase in the lowest eigenvalue of the MIMO channel matrix—strong indicators of improved wireless capacity and reliability. We also compared these active surfaces to conventional repeaters, which amplify and retransmit signals. While repeaters can deliver similar performance under ideal conditions, they suffer from practical challenges such as self-interference and the need for complex, high-power deployments. In contrast, our simulated active RIS design avoids these issues while delivering substantial performance gains.

Broader Impacts: This research has significant implications for the future of wireless networks, including Wi-Fi 7 and emerging 6G technologies. Smart surface technology can be deployed in homes, offices, and public environments to enhance coverage and data rates without requiring infrastructure upgrades. In addition to our technical contributions, we engaged in outreach to inspire future generations of engineers, industry, by show-casing the smart surface prototype showcased at a Research Expo, including the news and media. This demonstration visually illustrated how the smart surface could improve Wi-Fi signal quality, helping students connect theoretical concepts with real-world applications. In addition to that, the outcomes of this effort are incoporated into our courses at ECE department. 

Conclusion: This project successfully demonstrated the potential of adaptive, polarization-resilient smart surfaces to enhance wireless environments. Our findings support a new direction in wireless system design that emphasizes environmental reconfiguration over infrastructure replacement. We recommend continued research into active, amplification-based smart surfaces, which offer the greatest promise for real-world impact in next-generation wireless systems.

abstractText:
Imagine working for a major American company with branches around the world. You are on a conference call with speakers from multiple countries with different native languages. Even though everyone is speaking the same language, misunderstandings often happen. Given that the common language is often not the native language for all speakers, the different accents may lead to communication issues. Many people assume that these misunderstandings happen because speakers hear sounds quite similarly to native speakers but have difficulty producing the speech sounds like a native speaker (i.e., their speech is “accented”), perhaps due to ingrained motor habits and/or less experience producing the sounds. But another possibility is that nonnative speakers produce some sounds differently from most native speakers because they actually hear those sounds differently. This research project seeks to understand how a particular speaker’s perception of speech sounds (such as the vowel sound in “ship” vs. “shape”) is related to that speaker’s production of the sounds. This is a particularly relevant question for second-language speakers, who often have difficulties with both perception and production. It also has ramifications for native listeners, who often have difficulties comprehending speech from second-language speakers or speakers of less-familiar dialects or with less-familiar accents. Better communication among speakers of a common language who have different language backgrounds and accents would benefit instructional contexts with international students, medical care settings, and extension of American businesses into new markets. 

This project uses a novel research paradigm to test subtle aspects of how people perceive their own speech. Speakers for whom English is their first (or only) language and speakers who learned English as a second language will be recorded naming a set of pictures. Each participant will then hear their own or someone else’s recording, which they will need to identify. For example, they may hear their own (or someone else’s) recording of “ship” and must select the intended word from one of four pictures: ship, shape, log, and lock. If perception is a source of communication difficulties, speakers of English as a second language should be relatively better at understanding their own speech (more accurate and faster at choosing the intended word) than the speech of others because it will match their mental representations. If they speak inaccurately because of motor difficulty, then they will find their own speech difficult to understand, compared with their understanding of native speech. Indeed, this pattern may also hold for native speakers, albeit at a reduced level, providing more general insights into the links between representations for speech perception and production.

This RAPID project supports the analysis of satellite data following the August 14, 2021, Haiti earthquake (M=7.2) by combining Sentinel-1 and ALOS-2 InSAR observations.  The analysis will allow preliminary interpretation of the interaction of strike-slip and thrust faults that rupture during the Haiti earthquake sequence.  Systematic release of preliminary and refined images as each new satellite pass occurs (~5-7 days) and as the aftershock sequence and supporting field work takes place. InSAR, along with aftershock relocations, will be critical to help define the fault geometry necessary for understanding the rupture and subsequent stress changes on adjacent faults. Updated images will be released right after each acquisition (https://topex.ucsd.edu/haiti_7.2/). Early distribution of these data to local field scientists informs geologic mapping that will contribute to collecting ephemeral data on surface slip. 

Higher accuracy InSAR observations produced using the GMTSAR package, with stacking and noise reduction, combining data from Sentinel-1 and ALOS-2, are critical for future modeling efforts.  The method increases the accuracy of InSAR line-of-sight (LoS) deformation maps while providing data products to help researchers identify ancillary fault structures with co- and post-seismic slip that will be constrained at large scale by available GPS data. The InSAR imagery can help resolve how significant the component of dip slip on the eastern segment of the Enriquillo Plantain Gardens Fault is and how its interaction with thrust faults is a major factor controlling this fault segmentation and thus impacts the seismic hazard in this trans-pressive boundary of the Caribbean plate.  This project will support a female graduate student who will process the images weekly.

projectOutComesReport:
Earthquakes pose a major threat to the people of Haiti, as tragically shown by the catastrophic M7.0, 2010 earthquake and more recently by the M7.2 2021 earthquake. These events both occurred within the Enriquillo Plantain Garden Fault Zone (EPGFZ) which runs through the southern peninsula of Haiti and is a major source of seismic hazard for the region. The objective of this project was to provide processed satellite imagery as early as possible after the 2021 earthquake to the scientific research and seismic hazard communities to learn as much as possible about the evolution of earthquake hazard following the event. The project used a technique called Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) to show how the ground was deformed during and following the event. InSAR essentially takes the difference of radar images of the ground surface before and after the earthquake. In addition to mapping the deformation due to the main shock, we provide InSAR images that show the evolution over the following two weeks of continued motion on the main fault and several faults up to 10 km away that are associated with the EPGFZ.

Broader Impacts: The information was provided to geologists and other Haitian scientists to support any field investigations, although access to the field was severely limited even to local scientists. Several meetings were held with Haitian geophysicists and international associates to provide and describe the information contained in the database and support further study. The dataset will be further analyzed in collaboration with Haitian graduate students and scientists at Facult? des Sciences Universit? d'?tat d'Ha?ti, and Laboratoire G?oazur, and will form the basis of a PhD thesis of a female graduate student at Scripps Institution of Oceanography.

We provide a database of images that can be accessed through the google earth software (https://www.google.com/earth/versions/) that is freely available and accessible to any user worldwide. The database (https://topex.ucsd.edu/haiti_7.2/index.html) contains kmz files that are easily downloaded and opened in google earth, with the original InSAR imagery and identified fault segments where motion was detected during and following  the earthquake.

This workshop will build on the widespread interest in the Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) data principles for Open Science to synthesize and develop a consensus about next steps for the FAIR movement in the U.S. among representative organizations and thought leaders in the country.  The workshop will bring together a diverse group of experts and representative stakeholders from data and research communities, U.S. funders and mission agencies, and science societies, to seek input on the most promising concrete pathways for expanding uptake, integration, and implementation of the FAIR Principles in research practice and services.  

The primary aim of the workshop is to produce a scoping report that can serve as an agenda for the most promising strategies and approaches for FAIR capacity development incorporating the voices of academia, government, and industry.  This will be an invitational meeting which will seek diverse participants who are outside the well-known public voices on Research Data Management systems and services, while also including leaders who are working at the intersections of data infrastructure development, domain sciences, and open science.  International partners engaged in related initiatives will also be assembled for perspectives and experiences that will inform US efforts.  The goal for the workshop is to structure it as a series of highly interactive facilitated sessions with specific targeted outcomes that will contribute to the project report.

projectOutComesReport:
The pursuit of open science includes emerging practices around data, code, and related research materials that will improve access to information about research and its outcomes. The FAIR principles articulate basic aspects of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse of research products, the metadata that describe them, and the identifiers that support linking them to each other, in and across the scholarly communication system. The promise of FAIR is that a broad increase in the application of the Principles will lead to efficiencies in scientific and scholarly production, and result in new discoveries and knowledge. The implementation of tools and technologies to make metadata, data, software and code, and other related products and processes FAIR will facilitate data integration, improve seamless service provision across resources and organizations; and, vastly improved (human and) machine readability of metadata and data that would increase reusability. 

Activities that lead to increased FAIR data capacity in the US will make for competitive advantage in our national research enterprise. Building networks of expertise among U.S. research communities working to develop and implement technologies for FAIR research products and services, and understanding current challenges to these efforts, contribute to the U.S. FAIR capacity. Toward these goals, a symposium was designed to gather the needs and concerns of the U.S. research community on approaches, implementations, and investments in FAIR data and code (and related products), introduce some European initiatives, and to further clarification of roles and responsibilities of the production and oversight of FAIR materials, tools, and services. Speakers and participants were drawn from academic, government, and private sectors; in addition to plenary talks and panels that covered a broad range of U.S. domain science efforts, leading experts in European FAIR organizations presented on successful initiatives underway there. Together, these virtual workshop events served to increase understanding and dissemination of leading FAIR developments and how they apply in the U.S., or cross-domain contexts. 

The "FAIR for US" virtual workshop and associated activities gathered input from across the U.S. research community on near-term achievable aims for the uptake of the FAIR principles in the production and dissemination of new knowledge. The symposium format served to strengthen and extend existing networks around FAIR data stewardship capacity in the US, and provided all participants with a better understanding of the landscape and replicable models for uptake and implementation. A scoping report that informs prospective, impactful community-led data initiatives is forthcoming.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of a robotic control that uses air. Rather than controlling robotic systems with microcontrollers and motors, the proposed technology controls commercial robotic platforms with air using minimal electronics. The control approach has not been used in a commercial robotic product to date but may decrease the manufacturing and assembly costs of commercial robotic systems while maintaining or expanding the capabilities of robots.  Initially, the pneumatic components will be used to control a robotic toy as a commercially-viable stepping-stone for powering and controlling commercial robotic systems with pneumatic circuits.

This I-Corps project is based on the development of pneumatic memory elements to control the movement of robots with air.  The robots move by pumping air through channels and embedded air-powered valves. Traditional robots require a motor to control every actuated joint while the proposed technology only requires one pressure source, such as a pump, to control multiple movements.  Recently published results demonstrate the use of air-powered circuits inspired by neural circuits found in animals, called central pattern generators, to control the rhythmic motions of a walking robot without using electronics. The robot was equipped with valves acting as inverters that cause a high-pressure state to spread throughout an air-powered circuit. The robot also was equipped with simple pressure-activated mechanical sensors to change the movement of the robotic appendages. The goal is to transfer this soft robotic technology into a commercially viable product.

projectOutComesReport:
Our involvement in the NSF I-Corps Teams Program has been instrumental in offering our team invaluable mentorship as we explored the commercial potential of our soft robotics technology.

Introduction:

Our mission is to inspire curiosity, foster creativity, and cultivate critical thinking skills among students by utilizing cutting-edge technology from the field of soft robotics. We are dedicated to transforming STEM education by utilizing our innovative inflatable soft robotic toys. Our toys combine the comfort of a stuffed animal with the STEM educational component of robotics. With our toys, kids stay engaged by building and playing with bioinspired soft robots that are hands-on and user-friendly.

Accomplishments:

Customer Discovery- We conducted an extensive series of over 200 customer interviews, providing invaluable insights into various market segments.

Market Validation- We received positive feedback from potential customers, affirming a strong demand for our soft robotic toys.

Business Model Canvas- We developed and refined our business model canvas, pinpointing key partners, revenue streams, and distribution channels crucial for our venture's success.

Prototype Development- We Iterated on our soft robotics prototypes, guided by user experience feedback gathered during customer interviews.

Commercialization Roadmap- We created a comprehensive commercialization roadmap that outlines key milestones, timelines, and resource requirements for the successful launch of our soft robotics toys.

Key Findings:

Market Need- We analyzed competing products and technologies on the market enabling us to identify opportunities for differentiation and establish a competitive advantage. Our research revealed a demand for flexible and soft robotic solutions in the toy industry, addressing limitations of traditional rigid robotic toys on the market. Kids prefer soft robotic companions that they can treat like pets, while parents appreciate the educational and collaborative aspects of the toys. By identifying various pain points and preferences, we were able to tailor our designs to specific customer segments.

Market Entry Strategy-We conducted pilot studies to confirm the best entry points into our target markets. For instance, we introduced different soft robotic toys into a school in the LA unified school district which contained a diverse group of students from different socioeconomic classes. In addition, we formed strategic partners in the toy industry that will be crucial in our product development phase.

Future Steps:

Funding Pursuit- Our next steps involve pursuing non-dilutive funding opportunities, such as PFI/SBIR/STTR grants, to further support our research and product development efforts.

Partner Engagement- We plan to build strategic partnerships with industry leaders, research institutions, and investors that will be crucial for accelerating our product development.

Market Expansion- We will then explore additional verticals and applications for our soft robotics technology. The same methods used to control soft robotic toys can be used to control other robotic platforms.

Conclusion:

Through our project, we've introduced soft robotic toys into schools, preparing students for the challenges of tomorrow's world. These efforts aim to inspire interest in STEM fields and provide valuable hands-on learning experiences. The NSF I-Corps Teams Program has played a pivotal role by equipping us with the necessary tools and insights to propel our innovative soft robotics technology into a viable business venture. Our soft robotic toys have broader applications, and through collaboration with research labs and students, we aim to bridge the gap between academia and industry by facilitating the commercialization of soft robotic technologies. We are enthusiastic about continuing this journey and bringing our transformative technology to market, driving innovation and making a significant impact on the field of soft robotics.

abstractText:
There is a noticeable sparsity of data on the internet that can characterized as being easily findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR). This project seeks to leverage reusable components developed for the Magnetics Information Consortium (MagIC) that follow the above FAIR data principles and that are repurposed in the Framework for Integrated Earth Science and Technology Applications (FIESTA). Using this new FIESTA technology, we will build two new online data repositories: (1) KARAR: hosting analytical data and geological age information collected using the K/Ar and 40Ar/39Ar techniques for the age dating of rocks and minerals; and (2) GCPDR: hosting multi-sensor data collected at close intervals in sediment/rock cores that provide information on the physical and magnetic properties of sediments and rocks. Information to be drawn from the KARAR serves a critical need for almost every geoscientist enabling them to discover and assess the quality of the best and most current geochronological information from a variety of different methods and sources. Information in the GCPDR provides yet another domain of researchers with access to basic physical information (e.g. density, color spectra, seismic velocity) collected in tens of thousands sediment and rock cores held in national and international core repositories, which provides scientists with inimitable “time-stamped” records on ocean chemistry, geohazards, environmental tipping points, climate change, extinctions, Earth’s magnetic field behavior, global elemental cycles, and more.

The containerized FIESTA approach is designed to be readily adopted by a broad range of disciplines and, by hosting FIESTA at the EarthRef.org cyberinfrastructure, this will remove a significant set of hurdles in developing and managing a long-term FAIR data repository for these scientists. The two new FIESTA data repositories will also lead to the development of improved education in data mining tools and the use of cyberinfrastructure by exposing data in standardized easy-to-use formats, including standards developed in EarthCube, and making data available on GitHub and EarthRef.org’s JupyterHub. Finally, the standardization of datasets will enhance capabilities for interdisciplinary geoscience research as it lowers the hurdles to linking data across different fields and finding new applications to help solve persistently challenging scientific integration problems.

projectOutComesReport:
Modern science is transdisciplinary, requiring compilation and combination of data from multiple sources to address our greatest scientific challenges. It also requires that scientific products—whether from theory, lab experiments, or modeling—are reproducible to verify published results. But transdisciplinary science and reproducibility are still not easily achieved, despite advances in cyberinfrastructure and online data- bases. To achieve these goals, data should be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable—following FAIR Data Principles widely adopted by publishers, scientists, and funding agencies.

Making data FAIR, and in particular reusable and reproducible, requires subdomain scientists to define their preferred data formats in standardized data models and establish online repositories that expose their data and make them findable-accessible-accurate-interoperable-reusable-reproducible in connection with other data repositories. The Magnetics Information Consortium (MagIC) database has achieved this vision and it is now up to the community to upload their data.  Therefore, as part of this project, we uploaded over 60 data sets, which are all now findable, accessible (Image 1) and interoperable and many have already been re-used.   In addition, to make data sets used in particular publications reproducible, we have demonstrated the value of making fullly functional Jupyter notebooks (Image 2) which document how each  figure was reached in at recent publication (https://github.com/ltauxe/Pleistocene-paleointensity-notebook/blob/main/pleistocene_field_asymmetry.ipynb).

abstractText:
The team will conduct high-resolution optical and spectroscopic surveys of young planetary systems in an attempt to directly image and collect high-resolution spectra of hot Jovian-mass planets. The team will use the upgraded Gemini Planetary Imager (GPI 2.0) on the Gemini North telescope and the HISPEC high-resolution spectrometer on the Keck II telescope. They will obtain the first high-resolution spectra of forming gas giant planets, offering a pristine view of their atmospheric structure and abundances. The team will also develop a novel educational component for undergraduate astronomy courses based on a planetarium-based program.

The GPI 2.0 optical survey will target very young stars in nearby star-forming regions in Taurus and Rho Ophiuchus. It will be the most sensitive direct imaging survey ever conducted in this region. Using the demographic information discovered in the first iteration of GPI, the team expects to detect as many as 10 new exoplanets during the epoch of formation, constraining the timescale of formation, migration, accretion histories, and planet-disk interactions. Follow-up observations with the HISPEC spectrometer on the Keck II Telescope will provide R~100,000 spectra across the entire near-infrared wavelength regime (0.9-2.5 μm). The team will investigate predicted science performance for the instrument and provide targets from GPI 2.0 for first-light observations with HISPEC in 2024.

abstractText:
In this project, the research team will facilitate the development of ethical and responsible research (ER2) instructional prototypes designed to prompt dialogue about ER2 practices in social and computing (sociotechnical) systems for health research. The ER2 instructional prototypes will be developed through a three-phased process that includes: (1) an assessment of existing ER2 training and practices in academic programs that provide training in human computer interaction (HCI) (2) interviews with health researchers who use/study/develop sociotechnical systems, and (3) conducting community co-design workshops.  Key contributions will include the ER2 instructional prototypes for use by those designing technologies for use in health research as well as recommendations for educational interventions/strategies that are anchored to stakeholders within a behavioral ecological systems model. This research will be of interest to health researchers, health care providers, and health care users and their families, as well as be used to inform the training of the health care workforce. 

The project will explore how ethical and responsible research (ER2) is cultivated in academic programs that provide training in HCI at the intersection of health research.  The research team will examine and document the current ER2 landscape of HCI and design school programs to identify strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats to introducing formal and ad hoc instructional activities to foster respectful sociotechnical systems design applied to health research. Using a human centered design process, the research aims to increase awareness of ER2 practices and related social responsibilities that occur throughout the day-to-day cycle of health research.  First, activities related to Phases 1-2 will generate academic contributions that include data from a systematic review of relevant literature and prospective interviews to examine ER2 attitudes and practices among and within human computer interaction and interdisciplinary design programs. These programs are targeted as these settings are where sociotechnical systems are being conceptualized and developed for use in health research and healthcare. Second, by creating a map of the existing ER2 training landscape, using an ecological framework, the research team will document how ER2 training is applied in practice (e.g., designing databases, creating hooks into the data, developing data visualization dashboards). This will shape strategies for implementation of an ER2 Toolkit for sociotechnical health systems research. Third, the instructional prototypes developed through the community co-design process outlined in Phase 3 will contribute definitions and examples to a "design space" for tools to promote ER2 training and practice in HCI educational programs.  In terms of broader impacts, the research will develop instructional tools and recommendations for ethics educators and the larger sociotechnical health systems research community that are anchored to the behavioral ecological systems model.  A long-term impact of this research is to promote dialogue among health researchers about the ethical, legal, and social implications associated with the (mis)use of sociotechnical systems in research.

projectOutComesReport:
Our project examined how awareness of ethical and responsible research practices (ER2) are taught in sociotechnical and engineering research environments that contribute to educating those who develop and implement the tools used being used in digital health research and healthcare. Across three project phases, we identified consistent gaps between formal ethics instruction and real-world research practices. 

Phase 1 (Literature Review and Expert Interviews) analyzed existing peer reviewed publications and conducted interviews with 15 subject-matter experts. We found that ethical issues in digital health research were often addressed superficially. Common challenges included ensuring informed consent in complex digital health strategies, engaging diverse stakeholders, and managing research data responsibly. Data management concerns were particularly focused on data reuse and third-party data sharing. 

Phase 2 (Expert Interviews on Education and Mentorship) revealed that current ethics education tends to focus on compliance and broad ethical principles rather than on applied decision-making in active research settings. Mentorship quality varied and few programs offered structured opportunities for hands-on ER2 learning or reflection within laboratories. 

Phase 3 (School-wide Survey and Follow-up Interviews) involved a survey of 151 faculty, postdoctoral scholars, and students, and in-depth interviews with 15 people who contributed to the survey. Results confirmed limited awareness and utilization of existing ER2 resources. Nearly half of respondents (47.7%) were unsure where to obtain ethical or legal guidance, and only 12% were aware of the school’s Research Ethics Toolbox. Participants expressed strong interest in more practical, embedded approaches, such as research-integrated ethics guidelines (55%), short in-class ethics prompts (44%), and peer review mechanisms for ethical reflection within labs (40%). 

Key outcomes: The project generated actionable evidence supporting the integration of ER2 training directly into research environments. Findings informed the design of new tools, mentoring models, and curricular strategies that embed ethical reasoning into everyday research practice. Collectively, these efforts advance the intellectual merit of understanding how ethics can be operationalized in interdisciplinary STEM fields and the broader impacts of preparing a new generation of engineers and scientists to conduct research responsibly, transparently, and in alignment with public values.

abstractText:
Coral reefs are large underwater structures composed of the skeletons of corals that support entire ecosystems. They also provide substantial benefits to society that are estimated to total $1 trillion annually. These benefits include providing  storm protection to shorelines, as well as supporting sport and commercial fisheries and tourism. Unfortunately, the global loss of living coral from coral reefs has resulted in greatly reduced benefits to ecosystem health and society. Coral reproduces by generating swimming larvae that must find a safe surface on the reef to attach and grow. This process has a low success rate because the underwater surfaces of reefs no longer support juvenile coral survival. Relatively little is known about the how coral reef surfaces influence coral attachment and growth. The goal of this research is to address this knowledge gap and develop engineered surfaces to promote coral larvae settlement through a collaboration of materials engineering, fluid physics, microbiology, and conservation biology. Engineered surfaces will be deployed and tested on floating underwater platforms that are designed to support growing coral attachment and increase survival of coral by increasing water flow and oxygen availability. Successful completion of this research will transform the field of coral reef restoration, resulting in improved nearshore water quality and increased reef resilience to climate change and ocean acidification. Benefits to society result from improved recreational and commercial fisheries, as well as tourism. Further benefits result from interdisciplinary environmental research training for college students and early-career scientists to improve the Nation’s STEM workforce.

During sexual reproduction, swimming coral larvae must locate an appropriate substrate on which to settle and grow. Unfortunately, fundamental knowledge about the role of substrate properties that control successful coral larval settlement is lacking. This knowledge gap is particularly critical as coral reefs are in decline on a global basis due to climate change, ocean acidification, and other environmental disturbances. The goal of the project is to address these knowledge gaps and increase understanding of the physical and biochemical cues that enhance larval settlement and growth. This will be achieved by a convergent research approach that includes materials science and engineering, fluid mechanics, coral reproduction, marine microbiology, and reef ecology. The specific research objectives designed to achieve the overall goal are to: i) tailor material properties to release organic and ionic additives from natural hydraulic lime substrates that enhance the attraction, attachment, and settlement responses of coral larvae; ii) quantify fluid-substrate interactions, attachment, and microscale coral larvae transport near diverse substrate topographies using computational simulations and particle tracking experiments in custom-built oscillating flume chambers; iii) combine state-of-art materials characterization techniques and metagenomics methods to determine how substrate properties alter the microbiomes and skeletal growth of juvenile corals during and after successful settlement; and iv) deploy and test engineered substrates on floating restoration platforms designed to keep coral away from low flow, hypoxic, and algae-dominated benthic environments. Successful completion of this research has the potential to transform the field of coral restoration science and facilitate the restoration of coral reef ecological function. Restoration of critical coral reef resources will have numerous ecological and societal benefits, including supporting fisheries and tourism economies, as well as providing shoreline protection. The project will provide convergent, multidisciplinary training opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students, and underrepresented students in the Mathematics, Engineering, Science, Achievement (MESA) program. Additional benefits result from the training of a new generation of scientists in crossing disciplinary boundaries to solve societal grand challenges.

projectOutComesReport:
Our convergent research team sought to advance in coral restoration practices and restore ecological function to degrading coral reef habitats. With this project, we addressed several of the critical challenges in coral reef restoration by developing sustainable options that can create cleaner nearshore waters and support productive subsistence fisheries.

Intellectual Merit

This convergence project merged materials engineering, hydrodynamics, marine microbiology, and applied ecosystem restoration to create fundamental knowledge about coral reproduction and early life history with the goal of accelerating coral reef recovery. We released significant publications identifying fundamental principles of coral reef materials engineering, including key properties that maximize performance like base material, ionic additives, microtexture, and geometry. We used this materials research to determine how substrate characteristics affect the outcomes of juvenile corals on reefs and on the suspended restoration structures (named coral ARKs). These outcomes included factors that promoted 1) coral larvae attraction, attachment, settlement, and calcification of juveniles; 2) the establishment of a beneficial and protective microbiome; and 3) deterred fouling organisms that compete, smother, and overgrow coral juveniles. Ongoing research and long-term implementation of our substrate engineering have relevance to diverse fields of research including antifouling, aquaculture, biofilms, bioactive materials, and tissue engineering.

Leveraging the collaborative team’s experience in coral reproduction and larval propagation, we developed a system for using untargeted tandem mass spectrometry to measure, classify and preserve hundreds of unknown compounds released by crustose coralline algae. The compounds, released by crustose coralline algae as a biproduct of photosynthesis, are known to induce the attachment and metamorphosis of coral larvae on the sea floor. Research from this project provided a method for identifying specific chemicals that induce coral larval settlement and incorporating them into restoration substrates. Our team also developed a methods protocol detailing the best sampling and statistical practices for characterizing the microbiome of early coral life stages.

Broader Impacts

Our past and ongoing work centering the role of microbes in coral reef ecosystem science has consistently addressed the importance of microbial processes in ecosystem-based management. This project supported a significant contribution to the conservation and management of coral reef habitats, producing an Annual Review contextualizing how chemical ecology is central to the health of coral reefs. An associated publication linked the growth of specific microbial taxa with the removal of a vast array of previously uncategorized exudate compounds released into the seawater environment by corals and common fleshy macroalgae in the Caribbean. We also demonstrated how the oxygen gradients of various reef habitats in the Curaçao reef system were linked to coastal geometry and physics.

This project also supported an ongoing collaboration with the Caribbean Research and Management of Biodiversity (CARMABI) program. Reef habitats on Curaçao are experiencing environmental pressures from overfishing, nutrient pollution, climate change and diseases (such as Stony Coral Tissue Loss, SCTLD). Our work focused on understanding the microbiological and biogeochemical drivers of coral juvenile survival is central to coral conservation efforts. Additionally, the project goals to develop sustainable substrates to enhance the success of coral restoration will be critical for successful management of coral reef ecosystems worldwide.

This project made significant advances in student training in ecological engineering, microbiology, chemical ecology and coral reef science. This grant supported the independent research of several STEM students, all of which have gone on to further professional or academic scientific careers. The work supported three PhD and two MS students. Additionally, four undergraduate theses were supported.

Finally, this project engaged extensively in outreach and communication programs with the American people. Media communication included articles in popular magazines, local news, and podcasts. Both students and PIs shared the results of this project at two international conferences as well as domestic conferences in California and Oregon. PhD student Emily Nixon developed the education program Under the Blue Line (UTBL), where she employs VR to enable SCUBA exploration in classroom settings ranging from elementary schools to undergraduate courses at UC San Diego. Supported by this project, Emily took >3000 community members underwater on SCUBA dives showcasing Curaçaoan coral reefs and the work conducted on island through the NSF ECO-CBET grant. The UTBL program recently expanded collaborations with the education department at CARMABI to restore the function in old headsets, and dive with Curaçao restoration collaborators, Reef Renewal and SECORE, to produce local education modules. This new content will be offered in Curaçao classrooms in both English and Papiamentu.

abstractText:
This project supports an oceanographic field campaign in the tropical Pacific to make high temporal and spatial resolution measurements from moorings and ship of the oceanic velocity, density, and microstructure. Observations will be made of westward propagating oceanic fronts in the presence of Tropical Instability Waves (TIW) to better understand their influence on mixing and modulation of oceanic internal waves. The proposed work has important implications for understanding the El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the role of the tropical oceans in climate. Education and outreach for this project will include mentoring a graduate student and postdoc, science presentations at local high schools, mentorship for Research Experience for Undergraduates (REU) interns, and participation in the Ocean Discovery Institute homework assistance program.

This project addresses the dynamic processes that govern the observed modulation of internal waves, and turbulent mixing, by TIWs in the equatorial Pacific and the potential effects on heat regulation and ENSO predictability. Mechanisms to be studied include radiation of downward propagating internal waves from TIWs, modulation of the internal wave field by TIWs, and the fate of the internal waves in the presence of critical layers. The observational campaign will employ moorings, ship-mounted acoustics, ship-based profiling systems including a rapid profiling CTD (fastCTD) and a turbulence profiler (Epsilometer), and three autonomous drifting wave-powered profilers (WireWalkers). Three moorings will be deployed for a year north of the operational 140°W Tropical Atmosphere Ocean (TAO) mooring to target the seasonal cycle in the TIW modulation of internal waves and mixing.

abstractText:
Computer simulations of galaxy formation are powerful tools to help understand, test, and predict the observed properties of galaxies in the local and extremely distant Universe. Given the large number of sensitive wide-area galaxy surveys that have recently started (or are soon to be underway) there is a critical need for simulations that model the formation and evolution of galaxies with the highest accuracy. The proposed research will build upon the group’s earlier transformative galaxy simulations by adding the effects of gas accretion onto massive black holes, extremely high energy atomic nuclei (cosmic rays), and magnetic fields. These efforts will additionally train graduate and undergraduate students, mentor area high school students, and produce animations for public shows. The team will continue an educational program for prison inmates.

This research represents the further development of a project started several years ago by the FIRE (Feedback in Realistic Environments) collaboration to create state-of-the-art hydrodynamic simulations of galaxy formation and evolution that included a detailed treatment of “feedback” from massive stars and supernovae. That work successfully reproduced a wide range of observed galaxy properties – masses, chemical abundances trends, and scaling relations – for dwarf galaxies up to approximately Milky Way sized (L*) systems. For more massive galaxies, an accurate treatment of the energy injected by rapidly accreting massive black holes (i.e., active galactic nuclei; AGN) is required. This is one of the primary updates to the original FIRE simulation code proposed here. Other potentially important processes, including magnetic fields and cosmic rays, and a new framework to track chemical abundances are to be implemented as well. These promise to result in new galaxy simulations with parsec-scale resolution that are more accurate and that allow predictions (i.e., “forward modeling”) for a wide range of physical phenomena, including resolved radio and gamma-ray emission, cosmic ray spectra, Faraday rotation in and around galaxies, the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect, and the dynamics of the circum-galactic medium. The FIRE team will make publicly available to the scientific community new modules for the GIZMO simulation code developed as part of this work, as well as data products from the project. In the area of Broader Impacts this project will support four graduate students, a dozen undergraduate students, and a number of high-school students involved in creating scientific animations. The team will also engage inmates in educational activities via a partnership with the Stateville Correctional Center.

projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual Merrit: This NSF-funded project supported the production and analysis of new cosmological galaxy formation simulations, which include sophisticated models for magnetic fields, cosmic rays, the physics of supermassive black holes and improved treatment of material ejected during stellar evolution. These simulations enabled a closer look at some of the key uncertainties in galaxy formation and helped answer questions that were not possible to address with previous generations of simulations. PI and graduate students at UC San Diego worked on the project with other PI institutions (Caltech, Northwestern, and Princeton) and with broader FIRE collaboration. In addition to advances in the understanding of galaxy formation, forward-modeling of observables enabled direct constraints of uncertain processes in galaxy formation. We have shown that the joint evolution of stellar feedback, cosmic rays, and magnetic fields can explain gamma-ray and radio synchrotron emission from galaxies and these observations in-turn constrain underlying cosmic ray transport. The team also showed the potential of gas absorbers in the circum-galactic medium and X-ray emission from the hot halo gas to constrain the transport of cosmic rays. We have further constrained the galactic baryon cycle by characterizing the gas infall and outflows close to galactic disks, including slow radial gas sinking through the disk that enables long-term star formation in galaxies such as our own Milky Way. The detailed analysis uncovered the role of gravity and feedback from supernovae in the transport of angular momentum outward, which causes continuous gas flow inward. Finally, PI and his group made significant advances in self-consistent modeling of dust evolution in galaxies that explained the dominant role of accretion of gaseous metals for dust growth and depletions of different metal species onto dust grains. In the future, these models will enable more accurate calculations of emergent, dust-obscured light from galaxies.


Broader impact: Graduate students funded by this grant were mentored by the PI (and co-mentored by the other three PIs) and were trained in astrophysics research and physics related to hydrodynamical and non-thermal interactions of gas and plasma. The students also gained extensive experience in running massively parallel simulations on supercomputers and in general computing and data analysis. The PI delivered public talk at a local minority-serving community college and and students participated in public science outreach. The visualizations developed by the FIRE collaboration are broadly distributed to the public (including via FIRE collaboration web-page) and are used in teaching, talks, and featured in planetarium and television shows. The team has publicly released a large number of outputs from a range of FIRE simulations enabling a broad use of the products from this project by the scientific community.

abstractText:
Optimization techniques are useful for solving problems in economics, telecommunications, quantum physics, and other fields. This project involves Lagrange multiplier expression methods for optimization, which are use useful in computing. The project identifies and aims to solve various research tasks from the field of optimization within computational mathematics and related areas. The research topics of this project have broad applications in many areas of STEM. The computational methodology produced by this project will be highly useful in applications such as game theory, power allocation, environment pollution control, quantum entanglement, and tensor optimization. This project will also involve training and education for young scholars.

This project aims to solve various research problems in optimization relevant for the applications. Specifically, the project will involve Lagrange multiplier expressions which provide useful framework within computational mathematics. Expressing Lagrange multipliers in terms of objective and constraining functions is an important issue in optimization. Tight convex relaxation is efficient for solving computational questions.  The research topics include polynomial optimization, convex algebraic geometry, moment and tensor problems, bilevel optimization, generalized Nash equilibrium problems, stochastic optimization, tensor computation, tensor optimization, and other related problems. The project will address computational questions involving polynomials, matrices, moments and tensors, frequently appearing from various applications.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
This project works on Lagrange multiplier expression methods for solving various optimization problems. We use Lagrange multiplier expressions to give tight moment sum-of-squares type relaxations. Expressing Lagrange multipliers in terms of objective and constraining functions is a new technique for solving optimization problems. The PI and his team members have made important advances in the following research subjects: polynomial optimization relaxations for generalized semi-infinite programs, PLMEs and disjunctive decompositions for bilevel optimization, Lagrange multiplier expressions for matrix polynomial optimization, finite convergence of the Moment-SOS hierarchy for matrix constrained optimization, Nash equilibrium problems of polynomials, rational Generalized Nash equilibrium, multi-objective polynomial optimization, optimization over the weakly Pareto set and multi-task learning, polynomial optimization over unions of sets, characterization for tightness of sparse Moment-SOS relaxations, loss functions for finite sets, polynomial approximation for nonconvex two-stage stochastic programs, distributionally robust optimization with polynomial robust constraints. These results have been disseminated to scientific community. The project has made extensive efforts for training and professional developments. Several students and young scholars are trained for doing research on polynomial optimization. The research team holds regular meetings about research topics of this project. Various experts have been invited to give lectures. During the period of this project, a new book was written about moment and polynomial optimization, which has been published by SIAM. The book introduced most recent research results about moments and polynomial optimization, Lagrange multiplier expressions, tight relaxations, sparse optimization, bilevel optimization, Nash equilibrium, and various related topics. It is a good monograph for training students and young scholars who like to do research in this area.

abstractText:
Subduction zones, where tectonic plates are recycled back into the mantle as in the Cascadia margin of the Pacific Northwest of the United States, host the largest earthquakes and give rise to significant hazard through ground shaking, landslides, and tsunami. This project seeks to better utilize existing geophysical and geological observations from important “natural laboratories” (Cascadia, Japan and New Zealand) by merging them more fully into new, comparative computer models of system behavior. Developing new modeling software and integrating constraints is expected to lead to new insights into the physics of subduction zone earthquakes, what observations imply for future earthquakes, and, importantly, which observations are needed to improve our understanding of subduction zone hazards and how to reduce uncertainties about system behavior. The project will involve international collaborations, leverage past investments, and will contribute to defining future, optimal observational strategies. An interdisciplinary workforce of students and post-docs will be trained through research and educational efforts, and all project software, tutorials and “cookbooks” for subduction earthquake modeling will be shared with the community, contributing to advancing computational geoscience approaches in general. A program for precollege, undergrad, and early grad students will be developed to emphasize computational geoscience as an avenue to enhance diversity in the geosciences.

This collaborative effort seeks to integrate seismological, geodetic, experimental, and geological constraints for the Japan, New Zealand and Japan natural subduction zone laboratories into numerical models to advance our understanding of megathrust earthquakes. Forward models and a new numerical modeling framework for data assimilation will be deployed to get closer to versatile tools for data-driven, physics-based hazard assessment. The focus is on the evolution of fault stress and strength over a range of spatio-temporal scales, quantifying uncertainties and sensitivity to parameters. This will allow formulating best strategies for inferring relevant parameters from data in the presence of ambiguous physics, including optimal observational design within the ongoing SZ4D community effort. All code will be made publicly available along with cookbooks and tutorials, and a networked effort will establish new, quantitative links and leverage individual efforts greatly. FRES funding will support a growing community of solid Earth geodynamicists who want to deploy their models in a hazard and monitoring context. A focus will be on training and sharing material for interdisciplinary computational geoscience efforts, from undergraduate to post-doc and practitioner level. Project participants will develop sustainable pathways for participation and work to enhance representation and inclusion in the geosciences by providing new pathways of entry based on modeling and remote sensing to complement field-based approaches.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
